title: Confession
hook: the parent who already saw the broken lamp, waiting; Shantideva confesses to Buddhas who already know
tomorrow: can you be glad for someone who just beat you?

segments.voice: Yesterday: leaving everything. We go without any of it, so harm done for its sake makes no sense. I leave it all. Now the chapter gets to its name.
screen: `I LEAVE IT ALL.` → `NOW, THE CHAPTER'S NAME.`

segments.voice: A lamp is lying in pieces on the living room floor. The parent saw the whole thing from the kitchen doorway: the ball, the bounce, the crash. The kid doesn't know that. So the parent waits, and the kid starts talking about how the cat was acting strange today. The parent already knows. Everybody in the room can feel that the knowing isn't the point. They're waiting for one sentence. And that's today's puzzle, because Shantideva's confession goes to an audience that already knows everything.
screen: `A LAMP IN PIECES.` → `THE PARENT ALREADY SAW.` → `WAITING FOR ONE SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the odd detail. The whole second chapter is called a confession of wrongs, and Shantideva makes it to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, with folded hands. In his own tradition, Buddhas see clearly. They don't need the news. So why say it? Read how the chapter closes. He asks the guides of the world to accept his wrongs as wrongs. And then: since this was not good, I will not do it again. That's the answer to the puzzle. Confession isn't for the listener's information. It changes the person speaking. While a wrong stays unspoken, it stays half-owned: a cat that was acting strange, a story we tell around it. Said out loud, it becomes mine, with a name and a shape. And only a wrong with a name can get a promise attached: not again. Notice the tone, too. He confesses to beings he describes as full of compassion. It's not a courtroom. It's the kitchen doorway, with someone who already saw and is waiting for one honest sentence. Said out loud.
screen: `TO BUDDHAS WHO ALREADY KNOW.` · `ACCEPT MY WRONGS AS WRONGS.` · `IT CHANGES THE ONE SPEAKING.` · `NOT A COURTROOM: A DOORWAY.` · then, large: `SAID OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: With a pen and paper, write one mistake you've made recently, in one plain sentence, with no excuses attached. Under it, write what you'll do differently. Then put the pen down and sit with the page, the way you'd sit with someone who already knows.
Confession: owning a wrong openly, as the start of change. Not news for the one who hears it, but a turn for the one who says it.
Here's the line: said out loud, a wrong can finally be mended. That's chapter two, closed.

screen: `DAY 1465 COUNTS.` → `SHANTIDEVA'S GUIDE · 10 OF 50.` → `TOMORROW: CAN YOU BE GLAD FOR SOMEONE WHO JUST BEAT YOU?`

howItsDone: Confession has a place across Buddhist practice: Theravada monks and nuns confess faults to one another regularly, and Mahayana and Tibetan practitioners recite confession texts before images of Buddhas, often with prostrations.

fork.setup: at work you sent the wrong file to a client. your boss was copied and clearly saw. what fits Shantideva's confession?
options: say nothing; she already knows, so mentioning it is pointless.
explain why the system made it easy to send the wrong file.
tell her plainly it was your mistake, and what you'll do next time.
fork.reveal: that she already knows isn't the point. said out loud, the mistake becomes yours, and only then can a 'not again' be attached.

chat.says: i snapped a little branch off ông's juniper while watering. he hasn't noticed. do i tell him?
options: Tell him. Said out loud it's yours to mend, and he'd want to know.
Don't. He hasn't noticed, so telling him only causes him worry.
Wait. If he notices on his own, then you can explain what happened.
chat.meaning: Shantideva confesses even to Buddhas who already know: saying a wrong out loud makes it yours, and makes a better next time possible.
